timeline.body: The Strait of Hormuz narrows to 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's daily oil supply passes through it, giving Iran the ability to threaten the global economy without leaving its own coastline.

Franklin Roosevelt met King Abdulaziz ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy, sealing an unwritten bargain — American military protection for the Saudi kingdom in exchange for stable oil — that has anchored US involvement in the Persian Gulf ever since.

The CIA and MI6 overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalized the oil industry, installing Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi as an authoritarian Western client whose secret police would torture dissidents for 26 years.

Britain announced its withdrawal from all military bases east of Suez, leaving a power vacuum in the Persian Gulf that Washington filled by arming the Shah as its regional gendarme under the Nixon Doctrine.

The Iranian Revolution toppled the Shah and replaced a US-aligned monarchy with an Islamic Republic whose founding constitution committed the state to supporting oppressed Muslims and liberation movements worldwide.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 diplomats hostage for 444 days, severing a diplomatic relationship that has never been restored.

Saddam Hussein invaded Iran with quiet American, Saudi, and Kuwaiti backing, beginning an eight-year war that killed half a million people and taught Tehran that its neighbors and the West would unite against it at any opportunity.
Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman formed the Gulf Cooperation Council to counterbalance revolutionary Iran — a military alliance dressed as an economic partnership.

Israel destroyed Iraq's Osirak nuclear reactor in a surprise airstrike, establishing the Begin Doctrine: Israel would use preventive force to stop any hostile state in the region from acquiring nuclear weapons.

USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard — Washington called it a tragic accident, awarded the ship's captain a Legion of Merit, and never formally apologized.

An Iranian dissident group publicly revealed secret uranium enrichment facilities at Natanz, exposing a clandestine nuclear program Iran had concealed for 18 years and triggering the crisis that defines the confrontation to this day.

The US invasion of Iraq destroyed Iran's most powerful regional adversary and inadvertently handed Tehran enormous influence over Iraq's new Shia-majority government, tilting the Gulf balance of power in Iran's favor.

Iran and six world powers signed the JCPOA, trading strict limits on uranium enrichment for sanctions relief — Israel's Netanyahu flew to Washington to lobby Congress against the deal, and Riyadh viewed it as American abandonment.

Mohammed bin Salman, newly appointed as Saudi defense minister at age 29, launched a military intervention in Yemen against Iran-backed Houthi forces — his first major act of force and a war that would kill over 150,000 people.

Trump withdrew the US from the JCPOA and reimposed maximum pressure sanctions, collapsing the diplomatic framework and pushing Iran to resume enriching uranium to 60% purity — a short technical step from weapons grade.

A US drone strike at Baghdad airport killed Qasem Soleimani, commander of Iran's Quds Force and architect of its entire regional proxy network, marking the most consequential American targeted killing of a foreign military leader in decades.

The Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel, the UAE, and Bahrain, constructing an open anti-Iran strategic alignment across the Arab world that Saudi Arabia was expected — but chose not — to join.

Iran and Israel exchanged direct military strikes for the first time in history, ending decades of shadow warfare through proxies and crossing a threshold that neither side's deterrence framework was designed to survive.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: Congress passed the Posse Comitatus Act to ban the federal military from enforcing domestic law — a direct response to Union troops policing Southern elections during Reconstruction, and a legal boundary that later debates about militarized immigration enforcement would repeatedly test.

The United States created the Border Patrol not to stop undocumented crossings — which were barely regulated before — but to enforce newly invented national-origin quotas designed to keep out Southern Europeans, Asians, and Arabs.

Ronald Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and banned them from federal service for life, establishing the precedent that essential government workers who refuse to work without fair conditions can be treated as disposable.

Congress amended the Antideficiency Act to require federal agencies to cease non-essential operations during funding gaps, turning what had been a bureaucratic formality into a mechanism that could shut down the government and leave workers unpaid.

Newt Gingrich's Republican Congress forced two government shutdowns over budget disputes with Clinton, furloughing 800,000 federal workers and establishing the shutdown as a routine weapon of legislative brinksmanship.

Nineteen hijackers passed through airport security checkpoints operated by private contractors paid barely above minimum wage — the companies had won their contracts by bidding the lowest price, and turnover at some airports exceeded 400% annually.

Congress created the Transportation Security Administration just two months after September 11, federalizing 55,000 airport screeners overnight and making aviation security a government responsibility for the first time.

The Homeland Security Act merged 22 federal agencies into the Department of Homeland Security, the largest government reorganization since the creation of the Defense Department in 1947, bundling immigration enforcement, border control, disaster response, and airport security under one roof.

ICE was carved out of the old Immigration and Naturalization Service and the Customs Service, inheriting their budgets and personnel but shedding their service functions — the new agency was designed for enforcement from birth.

TSA screeners were explicitly excluded from collective bargaining rights that other federal employees had held for decades, leaving them with no union protections when future shutdowns forced them to work without pay.

The sixteen-day government shutdown over Affordable Care Act funding forced TSA agents to screen passengers without paychecks, while members of Congress who caused the shutdown continued to collect their salaries under the 27th Amendment.

ICE's budget had grown from $3.3 billion at its founding to over $7.6 billion, and the Trump administration began deploying ICE agents in courthouses, hospitals, and schools — spaces previously treated as sensitive locations off-limits to enforcement.

The longest government shutdown in American history lasted 35 days over border wall funding, leaving 800,000 federal workers including 51,000 TSA agents unpaid for over a month while airports descended into hours-long security lines.

TSA screener turnover hit 20% annually — the agency struggled to retain workers whose starting pay of $17.24 per hour was among the lowest in the federal government, well below what the same workers could earn at airport retail shops.

The Biden administration finally granted TSA employees access to the same pay scale and collective bargaining framework used by other federal workers, ending a two-decade carve-out that had kept screeners as second-class civil servants.

ICE began conducting high-profile immigration arrests at airports, courthouses, and churches, explicitly reversing the sensitive-locations policy and turning spaces designed for civilian transit into enforcement zones.

Congress had triggered four government shutdowns or near-shutdowns in three years, normalizing a cycle in which essential workers — screeners, air traffic controllers, Coast Guard members — absorb the cost of legislative dysfunction with their paychecks.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
